demoSteps.label: Black stone in the corner
demoSteps.caption: Start with the stone in the corner. There are no intersections beyond the board edges, so those directions cannot be liberties.

demoSteps.label: Two liberties in the corner
demoSteps.caption: Only the empty points to the right and below touch this stone along a line. It has two liberties; the diagonal point does not count.

terms.definition: An empty intersection next to a stone along a board line; diagonal points do not count.

demoSteps.label: White's final liberty
demoSteps.caption: Black occupies three of White's neighbouring points. Identify the one empty point still touching White.

demoSteps.label: Black captures White
demoSteps.caption: Black fills White's last liberty. With no liberties remaining, the white stone is removed from the board.

terms.definition: A connected group has only one liberty left and may be captured next.
When a move removes the opponent group's final liberty, the group is taken off the board.

demoSteps.label: Black has one liberty left
demoSteps.caption: Black has only the empty point below. First check that this intersection is still available.

demoSteps.label: Black extends to connect
demoSteps.caption: After Black extends downward, the two black stones form one group. Count the liberties of the connected group again.

terms.definition: Play next to your own group along a line, connecting the new stone and then recounting the group's liberties.

demoSteps.label: Two black stones are connected
demoSteps.caption: The two stones on the left touch along a board line, so they already belong to one group.

demoSteps.label: A diagonal stone is a separate group
demoSteps.caption: The lower-right stone sits diagonally from its neighbour. It is not directly connected, although a diagonal relationship may matter later.

terms.definition: Stones of one colour connected along board lines. Diagonal contact alone does not join groups.

demoSteps.label: The point between two black stones
demoSteps.caption: Both black stones touch the empty point in the middle. Playing there can connect them directly.

demoSteps.label: One connected black group
demoSteps.caption: Once Black plays between them, the three black stones are connected. Count their liberties as one group.

terms.definition: An empty point touching two of your groups that can join them with a legal move.

demoSteps.label: Where White could connect
demoSteps.caption: The empty point between these two white stones would let White connect them on its next turn.

demoSteps.label: Black occupies the cutting point
demoSteps.caption: Black takes the middle point, preventing that direct connection. Whether White can connect another way is a separate question.

terms.definition: An empty point where the opponent could directly connect two groups; occupying it blocks that particular connection.

demoSteps.label: An empty point surrounded by White
demoSteps.caption: The central intersection is surrounded on all four sides. Black would have no liberty there and would capture nothing.

demoSteps.label: An illegal self-capture point
demoSteps.caption: Black cannot play at the marked point under these rules. The cross indicates an illegal move, not merely a poor move.

demoSteps.label: Before White captures in a ko
demoSteps.caption: The central black stone has one liberty left. White can play on the marked point to capture it.

demoSteps.label: A ko position after White captures
demoSteps.caption: White captures Black, but the newly played white stone has only one liberty. An immediate black recapture would recreate the preceding position.

demoSteps.label: Immediate recapture is forbidden
demoSteps.caption: Under simple ko, Black cannot recapture immediately at the marked point. Black must first play elsewhere.

demoSteps.label: Retaking after an exchange elsewhere
demoSteps.caption: After moves elsewhere, the ko can be contested again. The blue square marks White's previous point; whether this exchange is worth making depends on the whole board.

terms.definition: A move that leaves your group without liberties and captures nothing.
Under the simple-ko rule you may not immediately retake a stone if it recreates the preceding position.
A meaningful threat elsewhere intended to draw a reply before contesting a ko again.

demoSteps.label: Three connected empty points
demoSteps.caption: White surrounds the outside of Black's group. The three highlighted empty points still form one space, not two eyes.

demoSteps.label: Black plays at the central vital point
demoSteps.caption: Playing at the centre separates the two remaining empty points. In this enclosed example, they become two real eyes.

demoSteps.label: Black contests White's vital point
demoSteps.caption: White is also surrounded. Black takes the central point first; judging the outcome still requires checking White's replies.

demoSteps.label: A point that looks like an eye
demoSteps.caption: The centre appears enclosed, but the black stone above has only that point as its remaining liberty.

demoSteps.label: White can enter this false eye
demoSteps.caption: White plays at the centre and captures the black stone above. A space the opponent can enter safely is not a secure real eye.

terms.definition: An enclosed empty point or region inside a group.
An eye the opponent cannot safely occupy; two separate real eyes generally let a group live in these basic positions.
A space that resembles an eye but can still be entered or destroyed by the opponent.
A point that can significantly change eyes, liberties or connections.
